mcqs.q: Dental healthcare is best described as:
opts: A two-person endeavour — the dentist working with the patient, and the patient accepting the treatment
A one-person task done by the dentist alone
A purely technical procedure with no relationship
Something only the patient is responsible for
mcqs.explain: Dental healthcare is a 2-person endeavour: the dentist working with the patient, and the patient being able to accept (use) the work offered.

mcqs.q: For dentists to make contact with patients, care should be:
mcqs.explain: To make contact with patients, dental care needs to be easy, acceptable and accessible.

mcqs.q: Some patients are UNABLE to use the dental care offered because they are:
opts: Too anxious, impoverished and/or disinterested to attend
mcqs.explain: Patients who are too anxious, too impoverished and/or seem too disinterested to attend are unable to use the care the dental team provides.

mcqs.q: Dental professionals tend to experience the MOST occupational stress with patients who appear:
opts: More demanding or more anxious (‘difficult’ patients)
mcqs.explain: Dental health professionals still experience stress, particularly with patients who appear more demanding or more anxious — those described as ‘difficult’.

mcqs.q: Appreciating the dentist–patient relationship helps to:
opts: Reduce occupational stress and enable the patient to accept care
Eliminate the need for clinical skill
mcqs.explain: Appreciation of the relationship reduces occupational stress and enables the patient to accept dental healthcare.

mcqs.q: The psychodynamic model describes the dentist–patient relationship in how many aspects?
opts: Three — real relationship, treatment alliance, transference
mcqs.explain: The three aspects are the real relationship, the treatment alliance, and the transference.

mcqs.q: The ‘real relationship’ is best described as:
opts: An equal, adult-to-adult relationship in which the patient chooses the dentist for clinical skill
A relationship distorted by the patient's past
A relationship in which the patient is passive
mcqs.explain: The real relationship is an equal & unique adult-to-adult relationship; the dentist is chosen by the patient for clinical attributes and skills.

mcqs.q: Mrs W chose a competent dentist despite her dental anxiety. This illustrates the:
mcqs.explain: Mrs W's wish for a competent dentist was unaffected by her anxiety — a good example of the real relationship.

mcqs.q: The treatment alliance is a development of the real relationship but is additionally:
opts: Affected by the patient's anxieties about accepting treatment
mcqs.explain: The treatment alliance is a development of the real relationship but is affected by the patient's anxieties and concerns about accepting dental treatment.

mcqs.q: When a patient's anxiety is too INTENSE, the result is that they:
opts: Cannot depend upon or align themselves with the dentist
mcqs.explain: The intensity of anxiety may render it impossible for the patient to depend upon, or align themselves with, the dentist — so they cannot accept/use the treatment.

mcqs.q: Laura was so anxious she refused all treatment. Her case shows that intense anxiety can:
opts: Make the treatment alliance difficult for BOTH patient and dentist
Only affect the patient, never the dentist
mcqs.explain: Laura's anxiety prevented her using care AND made the dentist unable to function in the alliance (calling her ‘difficult’) until he adjusted his reaction.

mcqs.q: Which are recognised BARRIERS that distort the dentist–patient relationship?
mcqs.explain: Barriers such as dental phobia and costs can distort the relationship between dentist and patient.

mcqs.q: Transference is best described as:
opts: A repetition of past emotional relationships inappropriately imposed on the dentist
mcqs.explain: Transference represents the past — a repetition of previously emotionally important relationships inappropriately imposed by the patient upon the dentist.

mcqs.q: Transference is most closely associated with:
opts: Regression — re-experiencing childhood memories and fears
mcqs.explain: Within transference the adult patient re-experiences childhood memories and fears; it is intrinsically associated with regression.

mcqs.q: ‘Regression’ describes a patient changing from:
opts: An emotionally controlled to a less well-controlled emotional state
mcqs.explain: Regression describes the psychological change from an emotionally controlled to a less well-controlled emotional state — the dentist as ‘parent’, patient as ‘child’.

mcqs.q: In the transference, the dentist–patient interaction becomes one between:
mcqs.explain: Within the transference the interaction is between the dentist as ‘parent’ and the patient as ‘child’.

mcqs.q: Assertive Mr B felt ‘helpless like a little boy’ in the surgery, reliving a painful childhood filling. This is an example of:
mcqs.explain: Mr B regressed from an emotionally controlled state outside to a less-controlled state inside the surgery — transference with regression.

mcqs.q: What helped restore the adult-to-adult equality for Mr B?
opts: The dentist's awareness plus the treatment alliance (which exists outside the transference)
mcqs.explain: The dentist's awareness of Mr B's feelings, together with the treatment alliance (operating outside the transference), let him ventilate concerns and restored equality.

mcqs.q: In the ACTIVE–PASSIVE formulation:
opts: The patient is passive and the dentist active; dentist = caring parent, patient = cared-for child
The patient leads and the dentist follows
mcqs.explain: In active–passive the patient must be passive and the dentist active for treatment to be possible — the dentist is the caring parent and the patient the cared-for child.

mcqs.q: Mrs R overcame her anger and attended the eye department on her dentist's advice. This illustrates the:
mcqs.explain: Mrs R acted on the dentist's guidance by cooperating (attending the eye department) — the guidance–cooperation formulation, possible because of the treatment alliance.

mcqs.q: The MUTUAL-PARTICIPATION formulation involves:
opts: Two adults working together for common dental-health goals
mcqs.explain: In mutual-participation two adults work together for common goals — preventive dental care is a two-person endeavour between adults.

mcqs.q: Mutual-participation is achieved by:
opts: Encouraging the patient to be active and take responsibility for their own dental health
Telling the patient to stay silent
mcqs.explain: It is achieved by encouraging the patient to be active, use the information exchange, and take responsibility for their own dental health; MI may be used here.

mcqs.q: Motivational interviewing (MI) is best described as:
opts: A method/style of communication and counselling for patients
mcqs.explain: MI is a method of communication — a style or method of counselling patients.

mcqs.q: Motivational interviewing fits most naturally within which formulation?
mcqs.explain: Techniques such as motivational interviewing may be used in the mutual-participation model, where the patient is active and takes responsibility.

mcqs.q: In the real relationship, the dentist is chosen by the patient because of the dentist's:
mcqs.explain: In the adult-to-adult real relationship, the dentist has been chosen by the patient because of his clinical attributes and skills.

mcqs.q: Dental healthcare maintains the EQUALITY of the relationship when it acknowledges:
opts: The real relationship, the treatment alliance and the transference within a dynamic framework
mcqs.explain: Care that acknowledges the real relationship, treatment alliance and transference within a dynamic framework maintains the equality of the dentist–patient relationship.

mcqs.q: The treatment alliance is important because, without it, the patient would be:
opts: Able to ignore the dentist safely
mcqs.explain: If the treatment alliance were not in operation, the patient would be unable to accept dental care.

mcqs.q: In the treatment alliance, the patient's anxiety is said to ‘merge’ with the dentist's:
mcqs.explain: In the treatment alliance the patient's concerns and anxiety about treatment seem to merge with the dentist's clinical and patient-management skills.

mcqs.q: Which statement about transference is TRUE?
opts: It develops with time and represents the past
It is present instantly and represents the future
It is the same as the real relationship
It is purely a technical matter
mcqs.explain: Transference develops with time and represents the past — a repetition of earlier emotionally important relationships.

mcqs.q: According to the mutual-participation model, preventive dental care must be:
opts: Carried out by the dentist alone
mcqs.explain: In mutual-participation two adults work together for common goals — preventive dental care must be a two-person endeavour between adults.

saqs.q: Define the treatment alliance and explain why it is important.
saqs.a: The treatment alliance is an equal, adult-to-adult relationship that develops from the real relationship but is affected by the patient's anxieties about accepting treatment; the patient's concerns ‘merge’ with the dentist's clinical & management skills. It is important because without it the patient is unable to accept dental care.

saqs.q: List and briefly describe the three aspects of the psychodynamic model.
saqs.a: Real relationship = equal adult-to-adult relationship (dentist chosen for clinical skill). Treatment alliance = working together, affected by the patient's anxieties about treatment. Transference = the past repeated and inappropriately imposed on the dentist (childhood fears, regression, parent/child).

saqs.q: What is transference, and what is meant by regression?
saqs.a: Transference develops with time and represents the past — a repetition of previously important emotional relationships inappropriately imposed on the dentist. Regression is the change from an emotionally controlled to a less well-controlled emotional state, so the dentist becomes the ‘parent’ and the patient the ‘child’.

saqs.q: Describe the three formulations of the dentist–patient relationship.
saqs.a: Active–passive: patient passive, dentist active (caring parent / cared-for child). Guidance–cooperation: the patient acts on the dentist's guidance by cooperating. Mutual-participation: two adults work together for common goals; the patient is active and responsible (preventive care is a two-person endeavour).

saqs.q: Using Laura's case, explain how intense anxiety affects the treatment alliance.
saqs.a: Laura's anxiety was so intense she could not depend on / align with the dentist and refused treatment. Her anxiety also affected the dentist, who could not function in the alliance and called her ‘difficult’. Only after he realised his reaction was inappropriate and discussed her fears could a treatment alliance form and a plan be made — so intense anxiety disrupts the alliance for both parties.

saqs.q: What is motivational interviewing and within which formulation does it best fit?
saqs.a: Motivational interviewing (MI) is a method/style of communication and counselling patients. It best fits the mutual-participation formulation, where the patient is encouraged to be active and take responsibility for their own dental health.
